claims.text: Coating tungsten particles with a thin, conformal graphene interphase before consolidation will increase the thermal conductivity of a W–Cu composite.
The graphene-coated W–Cu composite will maintain mechanical durability.
The graphene-coated W–Cu composite will retain irradiation resistance.
A thin graphene coating can be deposited on tungsten particles by chemical vapor deposition before mixing with copper powder and consolidation.
The particle coating will create a graphene interphase at the tungsten–copper interface.
Graphene has ultrahigh thermal conductivity.
The graphene interphase will form a well-bonded, electronically continuous bridge across the tungsten–copper interface.
The uncoated tungsten–copper interface is thermally resistive.
The graphene bridge will reduce interfacial phonon scattering.
The graphene bridge will reduce interfacial electron scattering.
Reduced interfacial phonon and electron scattering will increase the overall thermal conductivity of the W–Cu composite.
The robust and stable structure of the graphene interphase will preserve the composite's mechanical strength.
The robust and stable structure of the graphene interphase will preserve irradiation resistance.
The graphene-coated composite will have higher thermal conductivity than an otherwise comparable uncoated W–Cu composite.
The graphene-coated composite's mechanical performance will remain comparable to that of the uncoated baseline.
The graphene-coated composite's irradiation performance will remain comparable to that of the uncoated baseline.
The hypothesized benefits require a uniform graphene coating only a few atomic layers thick.
A sufficiently thick graphene coating could act as a weak interface under mechanical loading.
Excess coating thickness or coating-process defects could prevent the predicted benefits.
The coating's optimal thickness and long-term stability under fusion-reactor irradiation are uncertain.
